scenario: AITA for just being myself? | I'm (23M) British and have lived all my life in the UK up until recently, and I'd consider myself to be your typical Brit. I've always lived my life the way I've felt comfortable with and I try to stay true to myself. My humour and personality is very 'British', I make awful, dark jokes, I'll offend you, myself, everyone. Always joking and it's blatantly obvious but I'm serious and professional when I need to be, I support my friends no matter what, even if I constantly insult them. Almost everyone I know is like this, and I've lived in two different cities and been to uni so I know a wide variety of people. Never had any problem with it, I'm always open and honest about who I am. I've always thought this was perfectly normal. Almost everyone I would consider an acquaintance; male or female, young or old is more or less the same. I moved to the US 3 months ago for work on a 12-month contract with the option to extend it to permanent. I understand that the cultural differences are huge, but I just feel like I don't fit in at all. Everyone's so fucking nice and fake and woke. I'm young so for me the most important thing is to have fun and have a laugh. I can't do this here, the sense of humour is so shit and childish and unfunny. At first, I didn't really change my personality until I realised calling people cunts in a friendly manner within 10 minutes of meeting them isn't acceptable here, but that's fair enough, cultural differences and whatnot so I changed. I toned it down a lot but I still struggle to fit in, whether it's with colleagues or friends. I've made acquaintances with my flatmates' mates and about 10 of us were out for a drink and although I've toned my personality down so much, some of them pulled me up and said that they think I'm an AH and don't enjoy my company or my personality. A few others agreed and I feel shit now. My flatmates quite like my personality and said they far prefer the way I am to some of their other friends. One of them works with me and is one of about 3 colleagues that actually likes me. I don't want to change who I am for other people, esp when I haven't had to before. I lost it at one of my colleagues yesterday after work who said 'yeah you're an AH and just can't be nice to people' because that's so untrue. My way of of being friendly and nice is by being a cunt, everyone back home knows that and are the same. I don't want to change who I am but I just feel I don't fit in - hardly anybody shares similar interests or humour. Americans can't drink so I can't even bond with people that way to maybe get them to see it's just who I am. Having seen how fake so many people are, I can guarantee I'm a more caring, loyal individual than most of them. They all love to talk the talk but at the end of the day, most of them are snakes anyway. I love my work and there's so so much more career potential for what I do in the US. I don't want to go back home but I feel I have to. Am I an AH for just being me?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the person in this scenario is being an asshole (AITA) for just being themselves. Let me break this down step by step. First, the person is a 23-year-old British man who has moved to the US for work. He's been there for three months and is on a 12-month contract. He mentions that he's always been himself, with a very British sense of humor, which includes dark jokes and being offensive in a friendly way. He's comfortable with who he is and has never had issues fitting in back home. Now, in the US, he's finding it hard to fit in because people are "so fucking nice and fake and woke." He's struggling with the cultural differences, especially the sense of humor, which he finds childish and unfunny. Initially, he didn't change his behavior, but after realizing that calling people "cunts" in a friendly manner wasn't acceptable, he toned it down. However, even after toning down, some people still found him an asshole and didn't enjoy his company. He mentions that his flatmates like his personality and prefer it over their other friends. At work, only about three colleagues like him, and one of them even works with him. He had a confrontation with a colleague who accused him of being an asshole and not nice to people, which he took as untrue because his way of being friendly is through his British humor. He feels that Americans are fake and that he's more caring and loyal than most, but he's struggling to bond with people, especially over drinks, since he can't drink as much as he used to. He loves his work and sees more career potential in the US, but he's considering going back home because he doesn't fit in culturally. So, is he being an asshole for just being himself? Let me think about this. On one hand, he's trying to adapt to the new culture by toning down his behavior, which shows he's making an effort. However, he still feels that his personality isn't appreciated, and some people are pulling him up for it. He's holding onto his British identity and humor, which might not translate well in the US. On the other hand, he's in a new country with different cultural norms. It's important to respect and adapt to these norms to some extent, especially in a professional setting. While it's okay to maintain parts of his identity, he might need to find a balance between being true to himself and fitting into the new environment. He mentions that his flatmates like him, which suggests that he's not universally disliked. It's possible that some people just don't mesh with his personality, which is common in any social setting. However, the fact that colleagues and acquaintances are labeling him as an asshole might indicate that his behavior is coming across as off-putting, even after he's toned it down. He also mentions that he doesn't want to change who he is, which is understandable. But in a new culture, some level of adaptation is often necessary for integration. It's a fine line between staying true to oneself and making an effort to fit in enough to build relationships. In conclusion, while it's not inherently wrong to be himself, he might need to consider whether his behavior is contributing to the social challenges he's facing. It's possible that his British sense of humor and directness are clashing with American social norms, leading others to perceive him negatively. Finding a middle ground where he can express his personality while respecting the cultural context might help him integrate better without feeling like he's losing himself.
